transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah… thanks. I guess what finally pushed me to come in is work. I manage medical services, so I’m in EPIC a lot, and I’ll sit down to do a quality report—like clinic metrics, dashboards, all those numbers—and I really do mean to focus. I’m not trying to avoid it.

But within a few minutes, my mind is just… gone. Then I’m staring at the same line of numbers again and again, or I realize I missed the whole point of a meeting even though I was sitting right there. It’s embarrassing, especially because I should be tracking these things. I mean, I’ve been in healthcare long enough to know how important the details are—sorry, I’m rambling—but that’s the main thing. I’m having a hard time staying with what I’m supposed to be paying attention to.
When you think back to childhood, were you already having trouble paying attention?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, it’s funny because I was always told I was “bright,” so it kind of got brushed off. But I remember in elementary school, teachers would write things like “careless mistakes” or that I wasn’t turning things in, even when I knew the material.

And my mom—she had to sit with me at the kitchen table while I did homework, because otherwise I’d just sort of drift off or lose track of what I was supposed to be doing. Or I’d get home and realize I’d left the right book at school, which was always a whole production. I can still picture my backpack being this disaster… not that that’s exactly the point, but yes, it was there when I was a kid too.
Do you notice this same kind of trouble paying attention outside of work too?

Yeah, I mean… outside of work it happens too, but the work stuff is where it’s most obvious and honestly where it scared me enough to make the appointment.

Like I’ll sit down to do an EPIC quality report, or I’ll be in a clinic metrics meeting fully intending to follow along, and then a few minutes later I realize I’m not with it at all. I’m rereading the same numbers over and over, or everyone’s moved on in the discussion and I’ve missed the actual point. And then I’m trying to piece it together from context, which is… not a great feeling.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?

Um… worry a lot? I don’t know. I mean, I worry about work things sometimes, like anyone would, especially when there are reports due or something goes wrong with a clinic workflow, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around worrying about every possible thing.

I guess I’m not totally sure what counts as “a lot.” Like, I can get caught up in thinking about something, and then I’ll remember I never sent an email, and then I’m thinking about that instead—sorry, that’s not really the same as worry. So… no, I haven’t really noticed constant worrying across lots of different things.
When your focus gets this bad, are you also feeling depressed?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get frustrated with myself when my focus is really bad, and then I can feel kind of… discouraged, like, “Why can’t I just do this like everyone else?” 

But that feels more tied to the moment, if that makes sense. Like if I’ve lost half an hour on something that should’ve taken ten minutes, I’ll feel lousy about it. But I don’t know that I’m depressed in a bigger way. Although sometimes I’m probably not the best judge of that, because I’ll just keep moving to the next thing and then realize later I was upset.
Do you have the same trouble focusing at home?

At home… yeah, I think so, but it’s harder for me to measure. Like if I’m reading something or trying to sort through bills or whatever, I can realize I’ve been staring at it and not taking it in.

But honestly, the thing that made me come in was more at work. I can start an EPIC quality report or sit in a clinic metrics meeting meaning to really follow it, and then a few minutes later I’m just… gone mentally. I’ll be rereading the same numbers, or suddenly realize the discussion moved on and I missed the whole point. That’s the part that really got my attention.
Has there been a time when your trouble focusing was much worse only during a period when your mood felt distinctly down or different from your usual self?

I’m trying to think… I don’t know that I can point to a time where it was only because my mood was really down. Like, I’ve had times where I felt more discouraged or off, but the focusing problems don’t seem to neatly line up with that.

Sometimes I’ll be in a perfectly normal mood and still not absorb what I’m reading, or I’ll miss part of a meeting. And then other times I’ll feel bad because that happened, so it’s kind of hard to separate which came first.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed a distinct “down mood” period where that was the only time my focus got much worse.
Has this difficulty paying attention caused clear problems in your relationships or home life?

At home and relationships… I guess it’s not as clear to me as work, honestly. The obvious problems have been more like my delays at work are starting to affect clinic reporting deadlines, and then other teams are waiting on me, which feels awful.

And outside of work, I’ve had to pull back from leading parts of the volunteer health workshops I help with, because I can’t reliably keep all the planning pieces moving. I’ll mean to follow up or organize the next step, and then it just… doesn’t happen smoothly. So yes, it’s causing problems, just maybe not in the way people usually mean with relationships.
When you need to start a task, do you often find yourself unable to get going even when you want to begin?

Yes, that happens a lot. Especially with things like dense policy reviews or those long blocks of data analysis. I’ll know I need to start, and I’ll even want to get it done, but just the thought of sitting there with all that detailed reading and thinking feels… almost physically hard to begin.

So I end up putting it off until later in the day, which is ridiculous because then I’m more tired. But at the time I’ll tell myself, “Let me answer a few emails first,” or “I’ll start after this meeting,” and then suddenly the day is half gone.
Do your concentration problems tend to happen when something reminds you of a particularly stressful or upsetting event?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that pattern, no. I mean, stressful things can throw me off in the moment, like if something tense happens at work and then I’m trying to read a long document after that, but I don’t think it’s specifically because something reminds me of an upsetting event.

I guess I don’t really think of my concentration problems that way. They feel more… kind of general, like they show up even when there isn’t some obvious trigger.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

I don’t know… restless like physically needing to move? I wouldn’t say that’s the main thing I notice. I mean, I’ll shift around sometimes, but I think everyone does that, especially in long meetings.

Actually, meetings are a whole separate thing because sometimes the room setup is terrible, or someone’s sharing slides with tiny font, and then I’m distracted by that instead of—sorry, that’s not exactly what you asked. I guess I’m not sure I’d describe myself as “hard to sit still,” no.
Do you often have trouble keeping things organized?

I guess it depends what you mean by organized. Like, with my desk or files? I try to keep things in systems because in healthcare management there are so many folders and shared drives and versions of documents, and honestly the shared drive structure at work is kind of a mess anyway, so sometimes I can’t tell if it’s me or if it’s just… badly set up.

At home, I wouldn’t say everything is perfectly organized either, but I’m not sure if it’s unusually bad. I have piles that make sense to me until someone moves them, and then I can’t find anything. But I don’t know if I’d call it “often” exactly. I’d probably need to think about specific examples.
Do you often lose things you need, like keys, paperwork, or your phone?

Yes… that one, yes. I lose things all the time, or I guess “misplace” them, but it feels constant. My badge, handwritten notes, clinic folders—those are the big ones at work. I’ll have a flash drive literally in my hand before a meeting, and then two minutes later I’m checking my bag, the conference table, my pockets, everywhere.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I used to be the organized one. People would come to me for the right folder or the right paperwork, and now I’m the one hunting around saying, “I just had it.”
Are you often easily distracted by things going on around you or by unrelated thoughts?

Yes, very much. That’s actually one of the things that finally made me come in, because I’ll sit down to do an EPIC quality report, or I’ll be in a clinic metrics meeting really trying to follow along, and then a few minutes later I realize my mind is just… gone somewhere else.

And it’s not always because something obvious happened, though noise or movement around me can pull me off too. Sometimes it’s just an unrelated thought, like I’ll start thinking about a staffing issue or whether I responded to some email, and then suddenly I’m rereading the same numbers three times or realizing I missed the whole point of what someone just said. It’s frustrating because I go in intending to pay attention.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energetic or revved up compared with your normal self?

I’m not sure. I mean, I have busy periods where I’m running around a lot, especially if work is hectic or there are a bunch of meetings stacked together, but I don’t know if I’d call it “unusually energetic” or revved up.

Sometimes people say I seem like I’m moving fast, but usually it’s because I’m trying to get ten things done before I forget one of them. That’s different, I think. So… I don’t think I’ve noticed a period like that, unless you mean something more specific.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a longstanding pattern of inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood and persisting into adulthood across multiple settings, with clear occupational and volunteer-function impairment. Confirmed symptoms include difficulty sustaining attention, distractibility, task initiation/procrastination with effortful tasks, losing necessary items, and childhood careless mistakes/failure to turn in work. Anxiety, depressive episodes, trauma-related triggers, and manic states were not supported as primary explanations.
